# Comparing Post-Acute Care Outcomes between Home Health Care and Skilled Nursing Facilities: A Scoping Review

**Authors:** Fangli Geng; Kailin Xu; Yuchen Liu; Olivia I. Okereke; Sandra Shi

**Affiliations:** a.Department of Health Services, Policy & Practice at Brown University School of Public Health, Providence, RI | b.Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research, Hebrew SeniorLife, Boston, MA | c.Department of Global Health and Population at Harvard T.H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA | d.Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA | e.Department of Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and home health care (HHC) are two primary settings for post-acute care (PAC). There is growing interest in shifting care from SNFs to lower-cost home-based care, which may also be preferred by patients and families due to a more patient centered approach.

This scoping review aimed to: (1) identify conditions or populations for which SNF and HHC care models have been directly compared, and (2) assess outcome comparisons between SNF and HHC populations, with a focus on clinical measures and health care utilization.

Scoping Review

Older Adults aged≥65 years living in the United States

A search of PubMed and EMBASE was conducted from 01/01/1998 to 10/15/2024. Studies were included if they: (1) focused on PAC, explicitly comparing SNF and HHC, with HHC involving the receipt of care services; (2) reported patient-level clinical outcomes; (3) targeted older adult populations (aged≥65 years); (4) examined the U.S. healthcare system; and (5) were accessible in English. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers, followed by full-text reviews to determine eligibility, with discrepancies resolved through consensus.

Six studies published between 2011 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria. Most studies focused on short-term (e.g. 30 day) outcomes and older adults recovering from specific indications such as orthopedic surgeries. Outcomes included physical function, hospital readmissions, mortality, and costs. Although findings on hospital readmissions and functional outcomes were mixed, mortality rates showed no significant differences. Costs were consistently lower for HHC compared to SNFs.

Most comparative studies of HHC and SNF-based PAC focus on specific conditions for hospitalization, short term outcomes, and claims based measures. This review highlights the need for further research addressing broader clinical populations referred to SNF or HHC and longer-term, patient-centered outcomes.

## Abstract

Most comparative HHC and SNF-based PAC studies focus on specific conditions, and short-term claims-based measures. This scoping review highlights the need for research in broader clinical populations and patient centered outcomes.

## Introduction

Post-acute care (PAC) services play a crucial role in supporting the recovery of older adults following hospitalization.1 In the U.S., PAC is delivered in several settings, most commonly home health care (HHC) and skilled nursing facilities (SNF), which together account for nearly 40% of all hospital discharges among Medicare beneficiaries.2 The significant growth of post-acute care (PAC) over the past two decades reflects demographic shifts and increased demand for post-hospitalization medical and rehabilitation services among older adults.3, 4

Recent health policy and clinical trends have emphasized shifting care towards less intensive and lower-cost home-based settings, supported by innovations in telehealth, remote monitoring, and the “Hospital at Home” model.5, 6 Efforts are also underway to replicate SNF-level care within the home setting.7 These trends raise important questions about the comparative effectiveness of SNF versus HHC in supporting recovery among older adults.

While the comparative effectiveness of patient outcomes between Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRF) and SNF has been extensively studied,8, 9, 10 comparisons between HHCs and SNFs are less established. Fundamentally, SNF and HHC settings represent different care intensities and the degree to which there is reasonable overlap in populations that can be appropriately cared for in either setting remains unclear. Furthermore, the impact of shifting care from SNFs to HHC on patient care remains unknow. Understanding care outcomes is thus is crucial for guiding PAC referral decisions, aligning care with patient preferences, and informing Medicare payment reforms.

This scoping review aimed to: (1) identify conditions or populations for which post-acute SNF and HHC care have been directly compared and (2) assess outcomes of post-acute between SNF and HHC populations, with a focus on clinical measures and health care utilization.

## Methods

### Search strategy

Medicare’s Prospective Payment System (PPS) was implemented in 1998, which significantly altered payment incentives, structures, and the delivery of PAC.11 Therefore, our search focused on articles published from 1998 onward. We conducted a scoping search strategy from 01/01/1998 that incorporated MeSH terms and free-text keywords in PubMed, as well as Emtree terms in EMBASE. Parallel searches were conducted, with the detailed search strategy provided in the Supplemental Appendix. The search was last updated on 10/15/2024.

To qualify for inclusion, studies had to meet the following criteria: (1) focused on PAC, explicitly comparing SNF and HHC, with HHC involving the receipt of care services; (2) reported patient-level clinical outcomes; (3) targeted older adult populations (aged≥65 years); (4) examined the U.S. healthcare system; and (5) were accessible in English. Studies that did not meet these criteria were excluded. To supplement the database search, we manually screened the reference lists of eligible studies to identify any additional relevant studies. This process did not yield further eligible publications.

### Data Abstraction

Following the initial screening, the titles and abstracts of the identified articles were independently screened by two reviewers (FG and KX) to ensure relevance to the study objectives. A full-text review was then conducted for studies that met the preliminary criteria. Discrepancies during either phase were resolved either through discussion between the two reviewers, and if necessary, a third reviewer (SS).

A standardized data extraction form was developed to ensure consistent data collection. Extracted information included study characteristics (e.g., authors, year, sample size, study design), data source, population demographics, clinical conditions, and outcome measures. For studies which included other post-acute settings (e.g IRF or home without services) only the sample sizes reported for SNF vs HHC were extracted. While the primary focus was on clinical outcomes, data on costs were also extracted when available to provide additional context on the economic implications of these care models. Finally, we provided a narrative synthesis, structured to highlight patterns in study populations and outcome domains, in order to identify knowledge gaps relevant to future research.

## Result

### Search Results

A total of 2214 unique studies were retrieved from the initial search conducted in PubMed and EMBASE. The detailed selection process is presented in Figure 1. After screening the titles and abstracts, 114 studies were selected for full-text review. Of these, 108 studies were excluded based on the inclusion criteria, resulting in six studies that were eligible for analysis. Due to the low number of relevant studies identified and heterogeneity between studies, a descriptive review of the work was conducted.

### Conditions and Populations

The six included studies were published between 2011 and 2024 (Table 1). Three studies specifically focused on surgical procedures, such as hip fracture repair and joint replacement. One study (Werner) adopted a broader approach, examining outcomes for all patients discharged from the hospital. Another (Burke) focused exclusively on persons living with dementia. Lastly one exclusively studied fractures among community dweling women. Across studies, the populations consisted of older adults, with mean ages ranging from 77.2 to 84.7 for SNF patients and 73.5 to 82.7 for HHC patients. In general, HHC recipients were younger than those from SNFs.

Mallinson et al. (2011)12 and Mallinson et al. (2014)13 conducted prospective observational cohort studies with sample sizes of 154 and 103 participants, respectively. Mallinson et al. (2011) examined outcomes among patients following elective lower-extremity joint replacement surgery. The sample included a modest number of facilities across 11 states. Mallinson (2014) assessed patients recovering from hip fracture repair across 10 states.

In contrast, the remaining four studies by Lee et al. (2019),14 Werner et al. (2019),15 Burke et al. (2022),16 and Teigland et al. (2023),17 used large-scale administrative datasets from Medicare. Lee et al. (2019) evaluated outcomes after high-risk surgical procedures, including abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, coronary bypass grafting, aortic valve replacement, carotid endarterectomy, esophagectomy, pancreatectomy, lung resection, and cystectomy. Their overall study population included all surgery recipients regardless of discharge disposition, but explicitly compared outcomes by PAC received as well. Werner et al. (2019) included a broad sample of fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries discharged from hospitals, regardless of medical history or diagnosis. Burke et al. (2022) focused on Medicare beneficiaries with a diagnosis of dementia. Finally, Teigland et al. (2023) analyzed outcomes for community dwelling female fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries who sustained a fragility fracture between 2017 and 2019.

### Outcomes

The most frequently reported clinical outcome measures included hospital readmission, mortality, and functional independence (Table 2). Hospital readmissions were evaluated in four studies, with three specifically assessing 30-day readmission rates following hospital discharge. Three studies reported changes in mobility, self-care, and activities of daily living (ADLs). Additionally, costs were analyzed in two studies, which evaluated Medicare payments and overall cost ratios. One study examined readmission length of stay.

Regarding functional performance outcomes, findings were mixed. Mallinson et al. (2011) reported no significant improvements in self-care function after lower extremity joint replacement for patients in HHC compared with those in SNF, after fully adjusting for several characteristics including demographics, procedure, comorbidities and baseline self-care status (IRF-PAI score: 0.91; 95% confidence interval [Confidence Interval {CI}]: −0.31, 2.14) while Werner et al. (2019) found no significant difference in ADL improvement (−1.9; 95% CI: −12.0, 8.2) comparing patients in HHC with those in SNF. In contrast, to improve self-care outcomes for lower extremity joint replacement, Mallinson et al. (2014) reported a significant decline in self-care function (IRF-PAI score difference: −4.8; 95% CI: −7.48, −2.11) comparing patients with hip fracture in HHC vs those in SNF after full adjustment, although still did not report differences in mobility function (IRF-PAI score difference: −0.43; 95% CI: −3.26, 2.41).

For hospital readmissions during post-PAC stays, among high risk surgery patients Lee et al. (2019) reported lower readmission rates for patients in HHC vs SNF (14% vs 22% within 30 days of surgery). Teigland et al. (2023) reported a higher readmission rate for HHC vs (7.2 admissions vs 4.5 per 100 persons per month and Werner et al. (2019), which used instrumental variable regression to adjust for selection bias, found a higher readmission rate among patients in HHC compared to those in SNF (difference: 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI: 0.8, 10.3). Meanwhile, Burke et al. (2022) found no statistically significant difference in readmissions between HHC and SNF (difference: 0.12; 95% CI: −0.15, 0.40). In the post- PAC period HHC had lower 30-day readmissions rate (1.6 vs 2.3 for SNF per 100 persons per month). Only Lee et al. (2019) also evaluated readmission length of stay (LOS); the authors reported shorter durations among patients in HHC compared to those in SNF (7.1 days in SNF vs 5.4 days in HHCl; p<0.001).

Two studies assessed 30- and 100-day mortality. Neither study found a significant difference in 30-day mortality. Specifically, Werner et al. (2019) reported a percentage difference of −2.0 points (95% CI: −4.5, 0.5) in 30-day mortality. Similarly, Burke et al. (2022) found no significant percentage differences in either 30-day mortality (difference: 0.03; 95% CI: −0.13, 0.19) or 100-day mortality (difference: 0.12; 95% CI: −0.14, 0.38).

Two papers examined costs, which consistently favored HHC care. Teigland et al. (2023) reported lower costs for HHC versus SNFs (cost ratio: 0.63; 95% CI: 0.63, 0.64). Werner et al. (2019) demonstrated substantial cost savings in the HHC group, including reductions in Medicare payments to hospitals (difference: −$1,766; 95% CI: −$3621, $89) and to HHCs or SNFs (difference: −$5,384; 95% CI: −$6,932, −$3,837), and total Medicare spending in the first 60 days (difference: −$4,514; 95% CI: −$7,150, −$1,879).

## Discussion

This scoping review identified six studies comparing outcomes between skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and home health care (HHC) in older adult populations. In general studies have focused on surgical populations, with only one study examining broader hospitalization diagnoses. Most studies examined only short-term outcomes including readmissions or mortality, with none directly examining quality of life metrics or outcomes beyond 90 days. Very few, small studies were conducted prospectively, and no randomized trials were found. Collectively, these studies reveal important opportunities to enhance the evidence on post-acute care (PAC) effectiveness, particularly in guiding care transitions and informing policy reforms.

This review uncovered major gaps in the literature regarding post-acute care for salient medical conditions and diagnosis among older adults. Most studies examined a specific acute diagnosis (e.g., hip fracture) or population (e.g., persons living with dementia). Heart failure and shock, cellulitis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which are among the top ten diseases that prompt referral to PAC facilities, were not explicitly examined in any the studies we reviewed.18 Notably, none of the studies were conducted post COVID-19 pandemic, an event that significantly influenced healthcare delivery and outcomes, particularly in PAC settings.19 Post-pandemic research is essential to examine the long-term impacts of COVID-19 on recovery trajectories, healthcare costs, and patient outcomes.

Most included studies used Medicare FFS claims data, and only two studies, Mallinson et al. (2011, 2014), used prospective cohort designs with primary data collection. These were small in sample size and focused on orthopedic procedures. Administrative claims data, such as Medicare claims, offer significant advantages for studying utilization and costs across large populations. For these studies, the outcomes reported rely on data collected in routine care, including measurements from administrative data sets such as the Minimum Data Set (MDS). However these data lack details regarding more patient centered outcomes, such as quality of life or functional recovery. The limited scope of available evidence underscores the need for prospective studies across a broader range of PAC populations. Future research should incorporate more patient centered outcomes such as “home time” (days alive, not in a facility or hospital)20 and measures of frailty to gain a more comprehensive understanding of recovery and functional independence.21

Although claims data allow for rich information on healthcare utilization and cost metrics, a key challenge in directly comparing the quality of care between HHCs and SNFs lies in the absence of standardized assessment tools. Each PAC setting uses distinct outcome measures, complicating direct comparisons. The introduction of the CARE (Continuity Assessment Record and Evaluation) assessment data, introduced by the IMPACT act of 2014,22 designed to standardize outcome measurement across PAC settings, offers a promising solution. By enabling consistent comparisons, CARE data has the potential to address current gaps and enhance the validity and applicability of cross-setting research.

Short-term outcomes, which were the most common outcome measures, provide valuable insights into immediate recovery and care effectiveness. However, they fail to capture the full spectrum of a patient’s post-acute recovery journey. The majority of studies limited their scope to 30-day readmissions, future research should explore longer-term outcomes, such as 90-day readmissions or those occurring beyond the PAC phase. For instance, the work by Teigland et al. (2023) offers a valuable example, by examining readmissions after the PAC stay and providing broader insights into the sustainability of care outcomes.

The findings from the reviewed studies reveal conflicting results with regard to functional recovery. Differences in functional outcomes between HHC and SNFs likely reflect both underlying patient characteristics and the structural features of each care setting. While one study found comparable gains in self-care and mobility after lower extremity joint replacement, among those experiencing hip fracture HHC patients did worse. Due to low sample size, adjustment for baseline function is likely underpowered. However, those discharged to SNF were consistently of poorer baseline functional status and greater medical complexity, with conditions such as cognitive impairment, or pressure ulcers. For some, the home environment may promote greater functional recovery by enabling more natural physical activity and engaging family support. However, even among cohorts consisting of only dementia patients, no significant differences were found. Notably, HHC typically involves fewer professional care minutes, of both nursing and rehabilitation, compared to SNFs which consistently have higher therapy intensity. These complementary mechanisms underscore the importance of aligning post-acute care settings with patient needs, as both patient selection and setting characteristics significantly influence outcomes.

While some studies report fewer hospital readmissions for patients discharged to HHCs, at baseline those who went to HHC tended to be healthier. In analyses controlling baseline function and complexity, many of these differences were no longer significant. In fact, in the study by Werner et al. using instrumental variable analysis to mimic randomization, found worse 30-day readmission outcomes for those discharged to HHCs. These findings may suggest that for those who are sicker with more complex care needs benefit from the higher intensity, although more costly, SNF care. Furthermore, the differences between study findings underscore the need for robust methodologies that account for unmeasured confounders and selection bias.

Although cost was not examined in all studies, the data suggest that HHC is generally less expensive than SNF care. While it is possible that these were due to underlying baseline differences between the populations, most analyses adjusted for measured confounders including age, sex, and comorbidities. However unmeasured confounding may still be present, even after careful instrumental variable analysis. It is also worth noting that no study reported statistically significant differences in mortality. The inclusion of cost-effectiveness analyses could offer insights into the economic implications of different PAC settings and interventions, guiding policy and practice improvements in geriatric care.

This review offers valuable insights into the current state of knowledge regarding post-acute care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and home health care (HHC) agencies within the United States. As it is a scoping review we focused on describing the current state of known literature to map out knowledge gaps in patient conditions and populations, as well as identify inconsistencies between study findings. Due to heterogeneity of the studies identified, we were unable to provide a rigorous definitive answer to whether specific care setting may better suit particular patient populations. Nearly all of the studies were limited to fee for service Medicine within the US healthcare system. Thus, any conclusions, however broad, may not be generalizable to Medicare advantage populations or international health systems.

## Conclusions and Implications

Overall, the results for functional independence, readmissions, and mortality were inconsistent, underscoring the need for further research to address methodological variability and heterogeneity across studies. By evaluating the scope and quality of available evidence, this review provides an overview of existing evidence, highlights gaps in the populations studied, and outlines opportunities for future research to evaluate comparative effectiveness of SNFs and HHCs. To advance the field, future studies should incorporate richer clinical data, emphasize longer-term and patient-centered outcomes, and consider cost-effectiveness analyses to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of PAC effectiveness.
